items.question: Describe the salient features of Mauryan administration, drawing on the accounts of Megasthenes and Kautilya.
items.modelAnswer: Mauryan administration was a **centralised, autocratic monarchy** whose workings are reconstructed chiefly from **Megasthenes' Indica** and **Kautilya's Arthashastra**. Though power was concentrated in the ruler, the king was **assisted by a council** whose advice was **not binding**, and high officers were drawn from the councillors. At the top stood the **tirthas** — **Mantrin** (minister), **Purohita** (chief priest), **Senapati** (commander-in-chief) and **Yuvaraja** (crown prince). Revenue and justice were entrusted to specialised officials: the **Samaharta** (collector-general/assessment), the **Sannidhata** (chief treasurer and custodian of the storehouse), the **Vyavaharika/Dharmastha** (civil-court chief justice) and the **Pradeshta** (criminal-court chief justice). The empire was **divided into provinces**, each under a **prince (Rashtrapala/Kumara)** with capitals like **Taxila (Uttarapatha), Suvarnagiri (Dakshinapatha), Ujjain (Avantiratha)** and **Tosali (Kalinga)**; districts were run by the **Pradesika**, with **Rajukas** for land survey, **Gopa** for accounts and **Sthanika** as collectors. Separate arrangements governed rural and urban areas — Megasthenes famously records that **Pataliputra was managed by six committees of five members each**. The whole machinery rested on a **huge standing army** and an **elaborate espionage system**, while Ashoka later added **Dhamma Mahamatras** and **Rajukas** vested with reward-and-punishment powers, reflecting an increasingly welfare-oriented, paternal state.
keyPoints: Centralised autocratic monarchy; council advisory (non-binding); sources = Indica and Arthashastra.
Tirthas: Mantrin, Purohita, Senapati, Yuvaraja; key officers Samaharta (revenue), Sannidhata (treasury), Vyavaharika & Pradeshta (justice).
Provinces under princes (Rashtrapala/Kumara): Taxila, Suvarnagiri, Ujjain, Tosali.
District/local officers: Pradesika (magistrate), Rajukas (land survey), Gopa (accounts), Sthanika.
Pataliputra run by six committees of five members each (Megasthenes); backed by a huge army and spy network.
Ashoka added Dhamma Mahamatras and empowered Rajukas — a paternal, welfare-oriented turn.

items.question: "The Kalinga War transformed Ashoka from a conqueror into a moral emperor." Discuss the impact of the war and the nature of Ashoka's Dhamma.
items.modelAnswer: The **Kalinga War of 261 BCE**, described in the **Thirteenth Major Rock Edict**, caused enormous loss of life and became the **turning point** of Ashoka's reign. Overcome with remorse, he **abandoned the policy of physical occupation** for one of **cultural conquest** — a shift the tradition captures as moving from **Bherighosha (the war-drum)** to **Dhammaghosha (the drum of dhamma)**. He **embraced Buddhism**, framed **state policy on Buddhist principles**, and sought to win foreign lands **ideologically**, sending **ambassadors of peace** to Greece and West Asia and his children **Mahinda and Sanghamitra to Ceylon**. His **Dhamma** was not a sectarian creed but a code of **moral governance, social welfare and respect for all living beings**, embodying the ideal of **paternal kingship** in which the king treated his **subjects as his children** (the Kalinga Edict declares, 'All men are my children'). To propagate it he appointed **Dhamma Mahamatras** to teach dharma and secure people's material well-being, and **Rajukas** empowered to reward and punish. His edicts banned **animal sacrifice** (1st Rock Edict) and promoted non-violence, while the **Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra** purified the Sangha. Thus the war indeed converted a militaristic empire-builder into a **moral emperor** and India's **first global ambassador** — even if his pacifism and anti-sacrifice stance later drew criticism as contributing to the empire's decline.
keyPoints: Kalinga War (261 BCE), recorded in the 13th Rock Edict, was Ashoka's turning point.
Shift from Bherighosha to Dhammaghosha — physical to cultural/ideological conquest.
Dhamma = moral governance, welfare and respect for all life; paternal kingship ('All men are my children').
Propagated via Dhamma Mahamatras and empowered Rajukas; 1st Rock Edict banned animal sacrifice.
Buddhism spread through missionaries (Mahinda, Sanghamitra) and the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra.
Made Ashoka a moral emperor and 'First Global Ambassador of India'.

items.question: Evaluate the literary and archaeological sources available for reconstructing the history of the Mauryan Empire.
items.modelAnswer: The Mauryan period is unusually well documented for ancient India through **literary, foreign and archaeological** sources. The foremost literary source is the **Arthashastra of Kautilya** — written in **Sanskrit** in **15 books and 180 chapters** — which details the **legal, bureaucratic, economic and military framework** of the state and stresses the king's duty of **Yogakshema (welfare)**; though compiled centuries later, it preserves authentic administrative detail. **Foreign accounts** are invaluable: **Megasthenes**, Seleucus's ambassador at Pataliputra, wrote the **Indica** (surviving only as fragments in later Greek writers), while **Pliny** and **Diodorus** add data such as army strength. The Sanskrit drama **Mudrarakshasa** by **Vishakhadatta**, though of the Gupta era, dramatises Chandragupta's overthrow of the Nandas, and **Buddhist texts and the Puranas** supply dynastic and religious detail. **Epigraphy** is decisive: Ashoka's **39 inscriptions** — Major/Minor Rock, Separate Rock and Pillar edicts in **Prakrit-Brahmi, Kharoshthi, Aramaic and Greek** — give the ruler's own voice on Dhamma, administration and events like the Kalinga War. **Archaeology** — **NBPW pottery, punch-marked coins, burnt bricks, ring-wells** and monolithic **sandstone pillars** — corroborates the textual picture. Used together and critically, these sources allow a rounded reconstruction, though each (a lost Indica, a later-compiled Arthashastra) must be weighed for its limitations.
keyPoints: Arthashastra (Kautilya, Sanskrit; 15 books/180 chapters) — foremost source on administration and economy.
Foreign accounts: Megasthenes' Indica (fragments), plus Pliny and Diodorus.
Mudrarakshasa (Vishakhadatta) and Buddhist texts/Puranas add dynastic and religious detail.
Epigraphy: Ashoka's 39 edicts in Prakrit-Brahmi, Kharoshthi, Aramaic and Greek — the ruler's own voice.
Archaeology: NBPW, punch-marked coins, burnt bricks, ring-wells, sandstone pillars.
Sources must be used critically (lost Indica; later-compiled Arthashastra).

items.question: Critically examine the various factors responsible for the decline and fall of the Mauryan Empire.
items.modelAnswer: The Mauryan Empire began to disintegrate after **Ashoka's death in 232 BCE**, and within half a century the last emperor **Brihadratha** was **assassinated by his general Pushyamitra Shunga in 185 BCE**. Scholars debate several converging causes. First, a **Brahmanical reaction**: Ashoka's ban on **animal sacrifice** and superstitious rituals hurt the priestly class economically and turned them against the dynasty. Second, a **financial crisis** — the cost of the **largest army and bureaucracy** of the age, combined with **lavish royal grants to Buddhist monks**, drained the treasury, so much so that in later periods **gold images were melted** to meet expenses. Third, **oppressive rule** in the outlying provinces (complaints from **Taxila** under Bindusara and Ashoka) bred disaffection despite the rotation of officers. Fourth, the **spread of material knowledge** from the Gangetic core to Central India, Kalinga and the Deccan eroded Magadha's special advantage and enabled new powers — the **Shungas, Kanvas and Chetis** — to rise. Finally, **neglect of the North-West frontier**: preoccupied with missionary work, Ashoka failed to guard the passes, leaving India exposed to **Scythian, Shaka and Greek** incursions (unlike China's Great Wall). No single cause is sufficient; rather, the interaction of **religious-economic strain, administrative over-extension and external neglect** best explains the fall.
keyPoints: Decline began after Ashoka's death (232 BCE); Brihadratha killed by Pushyamitra Shunga in 185 BCE.
Brahmanical reaction to the ban on animal sacrifice and rituals.
Financial crisis: huge army/bureaucracy plus grants to monks drained the treasury (gold images melted).
Oppressive provincial rule (Taxila complaints) despite officer rotation.
Diffusion of material knowledge enabled Shungas, Kanvas and Chetis to rise.
Neglect of the North-West frontier invited Scythian/Shaka/Greek incursions — multi-causal decline.
